slides.title: Combining Tree Concepts

blocks.text: We've seen:
general trees, with multiple children per node
binary search trees, with a relationship among the elements but only two children per node
A multi-way search tree combines these elements
Each node might have more than two children with a specific relationship among the elements

Combining Tree Concepts
• We've seen:
– general trees, with multiple children per node
– binary search trees, with a relationship among the 
elements but only two children per node
• A multi-way search tree combines these 
elements

slides.title: B-trees

blocks.text: 2-3 and 2-4 trees are examples of a larger class of multi-way search trees called B-trees
The maximum number of children of each node is called the order of the B-tree
Thus, a 2-3 tree is a B-tree of order 3
A 2-4 tree is a B-tree of order 4

slides.title: Variations on B-Trees

blocks.text: A B*-tree is a B-tree that guarantees that each non-root node is at least two-thirds full
This avoids the problem of the B-tree being half empty
In a B+-tree, each element appears in a leaf, even if it also appears in an internal node
This improves the sequential access to all elements of the tree

slides.raw_text:
Variations on B-Trees
• A B*-tree is a B-tree that guarantees that each 
non-root node is at least two-thirds full
• This avoids the problem of the B-tree being half 
empty
• In a B+-tree, each element appears in a leaf, even 
if it also appears in an internal node
• This improves the sequential access to all 
elements of the tree

slides.title: Real World Applications of B-Trees

blocks.text: File systems: B-trees are often used to implement file systems, particularly in systems that need to manage large numbers of files and directories. For example, the NTFS file system used by Windows uses a variant of the B-tree data structure to organize files and directories. Database systems: Many database systems use B-trees to manage indexes and to store and retrieve data. B-trees are particularly useful in these applications because they allow for efficient search and retrieval of data, even when dealing with large amounts of data. Search engines: Search engines use B-trees to store the index of web pages. The B-tree data structure allows for fast searching and retrieval of web pages based on keywords. Operating systems: B-trees are used in operating systems to manage memory allocation and to organize file caches. For example, the FreeBSD operating system uses B- trees to manage the file system cache. Network routers: B-trees are used in network routers to manage routing tables. The B-tree data structure allows for efficient lookup of routing information and helps to ensure that packets are delivered to their intended destinations as quickly as possible. File transfer protocols: B-trees are used in file transfer protocols, such as the BitTorrent protocol, to manage the distribution of files across a network. The data structure allows for efficient tracking of which pieces of a file have been downloaded and which still need to be downloaded.

slides.raw_text:
Real World Applications of B-Trees
•
File systems: B-trees are often used to implement file systems, particularly in systems that 
need to manage large numbers of files and directories. For example, the NTFS file 
system used by Windows uses a variant of the B-tree data structure to organize files and 
directories.
•
Database systems: Many database systems use B-trees to manage indexes and to store and 
retrieve data. B-trees are particularly useful in these applications because they allow for 
efficient search and retrieval of data, even when dealing with large amounts of data.
•
Search engines: Search engines use B-trees to store the index of web pages. The B-tree 
data structure allows for fast searching and retrieval of web pages based on keywords.
•
Operating systems: B-trees are used in operating systems to manage memory 
allocation and to organize file caches. For example, the FreeBSD operating system uses B-
trees to manage the file system cache.
•
Network routers: B-trees are used in network routers to manage routing tables. The B-tree 
data structure allows for efficient lookup of routing information and helps to ensure that 
packets are delivered to their intended destinations as quickly as possible.
•
File transfer protocols: B-trees are used in file transfer protocols, such as the BitTorrent 
protocol, to manage the distribution of files across a network. The data structure allows for 
efficient tracking of which pieces of a file have been downloaded and which still need to be 
downloaded.
